::::::: {.content-visible when-meta="session2"}

## Welcome back

Last week you learned the basic building blocks: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and how a minimal jsPsych experiment is put together (`initJsPsych()`, a trial, a timeline, `jsPsych.run()`). Today, everything you build uses those exact same pieces — nothing from Session 1 is being replaced, only extended.

Today you will build **one experiment across the whole session**: a simple shape-categorization task, where participants see a shape and press **F** for circle or **J** for square. Each part of the session adds one new capability to this same experiment, so that by the end you have something that looks a lot like a real (if small) study — with practice, feedback, randomization, and repeated blocks of trials.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- Combine multiple jsPsych trial types (including images) in a single timeline.
- Randomize the order of stimuli.
- Show feedback that depends on the participant's previous response.
- Structure an experiment into a practice block and a main block, with the main block repeated multiple times.
:::

---

| **Objects & dot notation** (Part 3.3) | Each stimulus will be an object like `{image: ..., category: ...}` |

## Part 1 — Multiple Trial Types & Images {#sec-part1}

### 1.1 A new plugin: `image-keyboard-response`

Every jsPsych plugin follows the same recipe you learned in Session 1: a `type`, and a set of parameters that control what's shown and what counts as a response.

```js
const trial = {
  type: jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "images/circle1.jpg",
  choices: ["f", "j"]
};
```

Compare this to a trial from Session 1:

```js
// Session 1 — html-keyboard-response
const trial = {
  type: jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "<p>Hello, welcome to the experiment!</p>"
};

// Today — image-keyboard-response
const trial = {
  type: jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "images/circle1.jpg",
  choices: ["f", "j"]
};
```

The `type` is different — `jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse` versus `jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse` — because these are two separate plugins, each one built to display a different kind of content. `jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse`'s `stimulus` expects an HTML string; `jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse`'s `stimulus` expects a path to an image file instead. Beyond that one difference, everything else you learned about trials — `choices`, the trial ending on a valid key press — carries over unchanged.

### 1.2 Attaching extra information with `data`

A trial object can include a `data` field: a plain object (Session 1, Part 3.3) that gets saved alongside whatever the participant does. It doesn't affect what's shown on screen — it's a way of tagging the trial with information you'll want later.

```js
const trial = {
  type: jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "images/circle1.jpg",
  choices: ["f", "j"],
  data: { category: "circle", correct_response: "f" }
};
```

Here we're recording that this particular image is a circle, and that `f` is the correct key for it — information we'll need in Part 3 to give feedback.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
In `experiment.html`, add a `data` field to the example trial, recording its category and correct response. Then add two or three more image trials by hand (one per shape), each with its own `data` field. Run the experiment and confirm each trial displays correctly.
:::

### 1.3 A fixation cross before each trial

Run a few trials back to back and you'll notice a problem: one shape simply replaces another on screen, with no gap in between. It's not always obvious whether the display actually changed or whether your last key press was even registered — and participants have nowhere consistent to rest their eyes before the next shape appears.

The fix is one you've already seen: Session 1's Part 4 Challenge used a **fixation cross** — a `+` shown briefly before the real stimulus — to solve exactly this problem. We'll use that same trial before *every* stimulus trial from now on:

```js
const fixation_trial = {
  type: jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "<p style='font-size:60px;'>+</p>",
  choices: "NO_KEYS",
  trial_duration: 500
};
```

Nothing new here — `jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse`, `choices: "NO_KEYS"`, and `trial_duration` are all exactly as you used them in Session 1. The only change is *how often* you use it: once before every single stimulus trial, for the rest of this course.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
Add `fixation_trial` to `experiment.html`, and place one copy of it directly before each of your stimulus trials in the timeline (e.g. `[instructions_trial, fixation_trial, trial_1, fixation_trial, trial_2, ...]`). Run it and notice the brief `+` before each shape.
:::

## Part 2 — Randomization {#sec-part2}

### 2.1 Why randomize?

Writing out every trial by hand, in a fixed order, doesn't scale — and in a real experiment we usually don't want every participant to see stimuli in the same order (order effects are a confound). jsPsych provides a helper function for this: `jsPsych.randomization.shuffle()`.

```js
let stimulus_list = [
  { image: "images/circle1.jpg", category: "circle", correct_response: "f" },
  { image: "images/square1.jpg", category: "square", correct_response: "j" }
  // ... more stimuli
];

stimulus_list = jsPsych.randomization.shuffle(stimulus_list);
```

This is the same kind of array you learned about in Session 1 (Part 3.2) — just holding objects instead of plain filenames. `shuffle()` takes the array and returns a new version with the same items in a random order.

::: {.callout-note}
## `let` vs. no `let`
Notice `stimulus_list` only has `let` in front of it the *first* time, when it's created. The second line, `stimulus_list = jsPsych.randomization.shuffle(stimulus_list);`, reassigns the same variable to a new value — it doesn't need `let` again, because `stimulus_list` already exists. `let` means "create a new variable"; writing a variable name on its own (no `let`) means "update the variable that already exists." Using `let` twice for the same name in the same scope is actually an error in JavaScript. You'll see this same pattern again in Part 4, where brand-new variables get `let` and existing ones get reassigned without it.
:::

### 2.2 From an array of stimuli to an array of trials

Once we have a (shuffled) array describing our stimuli, we use a `for` loop — exactly like Session 1, Part 3.5 — to turn each item into a trial object:

```js
let stimulus_trials = [];

for (let i = 0; i < stimulus_list.length; i++) {
  let this_stimulus = stimulus_list[i];

  let trial = {
    type: jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse,
    stimulus: this_stimulus.image,
    choices: ["f", "j"],
    data: {
      category: this_stimulus.category,
      correct_response: this_stimulus.correct_response
    }
  };

  stimulus_trials.push(fixation_trial);
  stimulus_trials.push(trial);
}
```

Two new pieces of vocabulary here:

- **`this_stimulus.image`** — dot notation (Session 1, Part 3.3) to read a property off the current object in the loop.
- **`stimulus_trials.push(trial)`** — `.push(...)` adds a new item to the end of an array. We start with an empty array (`[]`) and grow it one trial at a time as the loop runs.

Notice `fixation_trial` (from Part 1.3) is pushed once per loop as well, directly before its matching stimulus trial — the same trial object, reused every time, exactly like `feedback_trial` will be reused later in Part 3.

Finally, we need to combine `instructions_trial` (a single trial) with `stimulus_trials` (an array of many trials) into one final timeline array:

```js
const timeline = [instructions_trial, ...stimulus_trials];
```

The three dots `...` in front of `stimulus_trials` are needed so that each trial ends up directly in the timeline, rather than `stimulus_trials` being nested inside it as a sub-array. You'll see this exact pattern, `[fixed_trial, ...trials_array]`, several more times today — it's worth recognizing, even if the mechanism behind it isn't essential to memorize right now.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Curious what those three dots actually do? (click to expand)

This is called the **spread operator**. It takes everything out of an array and lays it out individually, in place, wherever you write it:

```js
let fruits = ["apple", "banana"];

let without_spread = ["kiwi", fruits, "mango"];
// -> ["kiwi", ["apple", "banana"], "mango"]   <- fruits is nested inside!

let with_spread = ["kiwi", ...fruits, "mango"];
// -> ["kiwi", "apple", "banana", "mango"]      <- fruits is unpacked in place
```

Without `...`, `[instructions_trial, stimulus_trials]` would be an array containing a trial *and* a nested array of trials — which jsPsych wouldn't know how to run. With `...stimulus_trials`, every trial inside it is unpacked directly into the surrounding array instead.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
1. In `experiment.html`, replace your manually written trials from Part 1 with a `stimulus_list` array, `shuffle()`, and a `for` loop that builds `stimulus_trials` — pushing `fixation_trial` before each `trial`, as shown above.
2. Run the experiment twice in a row. Confirm the order of shapes is different each time, and that a `+` appears before every shape.
:::

## Part 3 — Conditional Feedback {#sec-part3}

This part introduces the trickiest new idea of the day: **a trial parameter can be a function, not just a fixed value.** Take it slowly, and don't worry if it takes a couple of read-throughs to sink in.

### 3.1 Scoring a response: `on_finish`

So far, none of our trials know whether the participant's response was *correct*. We can find out by comparing the key they pressed (`data.response`) to the correct key we stored earlier (`data.correct_response`) — but that comparison can only happen *after* the trial ends, once we know what was pressed.

jsPsych gives every trial an optional `on_finish` parameter: a function that runs immediately after that trial ends, and is handed that trial's own data to edit.

```js
const trial = {
  type: jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: this_stimulus.image,
  choices: ["f", "j"],
  data: {
    category: this_stimulus.category,
    correct_response: this_stimulus.correct_response
  },
  on_finish: function (data) {
    data.correct = (data.response === data.correct_response);
  }
};
```

`data.response === data.correct_response` is an **if-statement-style comparison** (Session 1, Part 3.4) — it evaluates to `true` or `false`, and we store that directly as a new property, `data.correct`.

### 3.2 A trial that reads the previous trial's data

Now we want a feedback trial whose text depends on whether the previous trial was correct. In every trial you've written so far, `stimulus` has been a fixed value — a string of HTML text (Session 1) or an image path (Part 1 today). Here, we need `stimulus` to change depending on what just happened, so instead of a fixed value we give it a **function**: jsPsych will call this function right before showing the trial, and use whatever string it returns.

```js
const feedback_trial = {
  type: jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: function () {
    let last_trial_data = jsPsych.data.get().last(1).values()[0];

    if (last_trial_data.correct) {
      return "<p style='color:green;'>Correct!</p>";
    } else {
      return "<p style='color:red;'>Incorrect.</p>";
    }
  },
  choices: "NO_KEYS",
  trial_duration: 800
};
```

Breaking down the new line:

- **`jsPsych.data.get()`** — returns all the data collected by the experiment so far.
- **`.last(1)`** — narrows this down to just the most recent trial.
- **`.values()[0]`** — unwraps that into a plain object we can read with dot notation, same as any other object.

The `if` statement here is exactly the same pattern from Session 1, Part 3.4 — the only difference is that the condition (`last_trial_data.correct`) comes from data collected while the experiment is running, rather than a variable we wrote ourselves.

::: {.callout-important}
## Order matters: define `feedback_trial` before your loop
JavaScript runs your code from top to bottom, in order — the same reason you must define a variable before using it (Session 1, Part 3.1). `feedback_trial` needs to exist *before* the loop that pushes it into `stimulus_trials`; if you define it further down the file, after the loop, you'll get an error saying `feedback_trial` doesn't exist yet. Keep `feedback_trial` above your `for` loop, the same way it's written above.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Common pitfall
Notice `feedback_trial` is defined *once*, outside any loop, and then reused after every stimulus trial. It doesn't need to know in advance which stimulus it's giving feedback about — it works that out for itself, each time it runs, using `jsPsych.data.get()`. You do not need (and should not create) a separate feedback trial for every stimulus.
:::

### Exercise 3

::: {.callout-warning}
## Exercise 3
Apply feedback directly to the 8-stimulus experiment you already built in **Exercise 2** — don't start a new file or a smaller test version, just extend what you have:

1. Add `on_finish` to each stimulus trial in your loop, so that `data.correct` gets recorded.
2. Define one `feedback_trial`, as shown above, *before* your loop.
3. Inside your loop, you should already be pushing `fixation_trial` then `trial` (from Exercise 2) — add a third line after those: `stimulus_trials.push(feedback_trial);`, so every trial now runs as fixation → stimulus → feedback.
4. Run your experiment and confirm you see "Correct!" or "Incorrect." after every one of the 8 responses.

## Part 4 — Practice Block & Repeating Blocks {#sec-part4}

### 4.1 Two separate arrays: practice and main

A typical experiment has a short **practice block** (with feedback, so participants learn the task) followed by a longer **main block** (without feedback, since we don't want to influence real responses). We build these the same way as before — an array of stimuli, shuffled, looped over — just twice, with one small difference each time.

```js
let practice_stimuli = jsPsych.randomization.shuffle(stimulus_list).slice(0, 4);
```

`.slice(0, 4)` takes just the first 4 items of the (already shuffled) array — a quick way to get a small random subset for practice.

The practice loop looks just like Part 3's loop, and still pushes `fixation_trial` then `feedback_trial` around every stimulus trial. The main block's loop is almost identical, except it does **not** push a feedback trial (though it still gets a fixation cross):

```js
let main_trials = [];

for (let i = 0; i < stimulus_list.length; i++) {
  let this_stimulus = stimulus_list[i];

  let trial = {
    type: jsPsychImageKeyboardResponse,
    stimulus: this_stimulus.image,
    choices: ["f", "j"],
    data: {
      phase: "main",
      category: this_stimulus.category,
      correct_response: this_stimulus.correct_response
    },
    on_finish: function (data) {
      data.correct = (data.response === data.correct_response);
    }
  };

  main_trials.push(fixation_trial);
  main_trials.push(trial); // no feedback trial pushed here
}
```

Note the added `phase: "main"` (and `phase: "practice"` in the practice version) in `data` — a small addition that will make it easy, in Session 3, to filter practice trials out when computing accuracy.

### 4.2 Repeating the main block with a loop

To repeat the whole main block several times (each time reshuffled), we wrap the loop above in another loop — a **loop inside a loop**:

```js
let n_repetitions = 3;
let main_trials = [];

for (let rep = 0; rep < n_repetitions; rep++) {
  let this_repetition_stimuli = jsPsych.randomization.shuffle(stimulus_list);

  for (let i = 0; i < this_repetition_stimuli.length; i++) {
    let this_stimulus = this_repetition_stimuli[i];
    // ... build trial, same as before ...
    main_trials.push(fixation_trial);
    main_trials.push(trial);
  }
}
```

Read the outer loop first: "repeat this whole block `n_repetitions` times." Each time around the outer loop, we reshuffle the stimulus list and run the *entire inner loop* again, adding a fresh set of trials to `main_trials`. This is a plain JavaScript loop doing the repeating — nothing jsPsych-specific yet. (Session 3 will introduce jsPsych's own built-in tool for this, `timeline_variables`, once you've seen why it's useful.)

### 4.3 Assembling the full timeline

```js
const timeline = [
  instructions_trial,
  ...practice_trials,
  transition_trial,
  ...main_trials,
  end_trial
];
```

A `transition_trial` and an `end_trial` are both just ordinary `jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse` trials — nothing new — used to mark the boundaries of the experiment:

```js
const transition_trial = {
  type: jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: `
    <p>Practice complete!</p>
    <p>Now the real trials begin. Feedback will no longer be shown.</p>
    <p>Press any key to continue.</p>
  `
};

const end_trial = {
  type: jsPsychHtmlKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "<p>Thank you — that's the end of the experiment!</p>",
  choices: "NO_KEYS",
  trial_duration: 2000
};
```

`transition_trial` tells participants practice is over and waits for a key press, same as the instructions trial. `end_trial` uses `choices: "NO_KEYS"` and `trial_duration: 2000` (from Session 1's Part 4 challenge) so the closing message displays for 2 seconds and then the experiment simply ends, with nothing for the participant to press.

### Challenge (optional)

::: {.callout-important}
## Challenge
Make `end_trial` show the participant how many main-block trials they actually completed, using the `phase` tag you added to each trial's `data` earlier.

You'll need one new tool: `jsPsych.data.get().filter({phase: "main"}).count()` — this takes all the collected data, `.filter(...)` keeps only the trials whose `data.phase` matches `"main"`, and `.count()` returns how many trials are left. Store this in a variable, then use it inside a `stimulus: function() {...}` — the same pattern as `feedback_trial` — to build a personalized closing message, e.g. *"You completed 24 main trials. Thank you!"*

For more on `.filter()`, `.count()`, and other data tools, see the [jsPsych data overview](https://www.jspsych.org/latest/overview/data/) and the [full `DataCollection` reference](https://www.jspsych.org/latest/reference/jspsych-data/).

This is a small preview of Session 3, where you'll use `.filter()` and similar tools much more, to compute accuracy and reaction time.
:::

## Bonus: Other Modalities — Audio & Video

Everything so far has used text (`html-keyboard-response`) or images (`image-keyboard-response`). Two more plugins follow the exact same recipe for sound and video: `audio-keyboard-response` and `video-keyboard-response`.

```html
<script src="jspsych/plugin-audio-keyboard-response.js"></script>
<script src="jspsych/plugin-video-keyboard-response.js"></script>
```

```js
const audio_trial = {
  type: jsPsychAudioKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: "media/tone_high.mp3",
  choices: ["h", "l"],
  data: { correct_response: "h" },
  on_finish: function (data) {
    data.correct = (data.response === data.correct_response);
  }
};

const video_trial = {
  type: jsPsychVideoKeyboardResponse,
  stimulus: ["media/circle_clip.mp4"],  // note: an ARRAY, not a plain string
  choices: "NO_KEYS",
  trial_ends_after_video: true
};
```

Notice how little is actually new: `type`, `choices`, `data`, `on_finish` are all exactly as you've used them all session. The genuinely new pieces are:

- **`trial_ends_after_audio` / `trial_ends_after_video`** — the trial waits for the media to finish playing, the same role `trial_duration` plays for a fixed time or `choices` plays for a key press.
- **`video`'s `stimulus` is an array**, not a plain string like every other plugin so far — an easy typo to make, since it looks like it should be `"media/circle_clip.mp4"` on its own.

::: {.callout-note}
## Debugging corner
Auto-preloading (Session 3 covers preloading properly) only works for audio/video files written as a fixed string or array, exactly like the image caveat you'll see with `timeline_variables` in Session 3 — if you dynamically build the stimulus path, you'll need to preload it by hand the same way. Also: video preloading is disabled entirely when running via a `file://` link instead of a real server (e.g. Live Server) — one more reason to always test with Live Server, not by double-clicking the HTML file.
:::

A working demo is provided in `audio_video_demo.html` — try it with Live Server (audio and video won't play reliably from a double-clicked file).

## Bonus: Button Responses

Every trial so far has ended with a key press. jsPsych can just as easily use on-screen buttons instead, via `html-button-response` (there are image/audio/video button variants too, following the same pattern).

```html
<script src="jspsych/plugin-html-button-response.js"></script>
```

```js
const trial = {
  type: jsPsychHtmlButtonResponse,
  stimulus: "<p style='color:red;'>GREEN</p>",
  choices: ["Red", "Green", "Blue"]
};
```

This looks almost identical to `html-keyboard-response` — `type`, `stimulus`, `choices` — but `choices` here is a list of **button labels**, not key characters, and buttons appear on screen for the participant to click.

::: {.callout-important}
## The one real difference: how the response is recorded
With every keyboard plugin so far, `data.response` has been the character key that was pressed (e.g. `"f"`). With `html-button-response`, **`data.response` is the *index* of the button clicked** (`0` for the first button, `1` for the second, and so on) — not the button's text. If you write `on_finish` scoring exactly like your keyboard trials (comparing `data.response` to a key character), it will silently never match. Compare it to a **number** instead:

```js
data: { correct_response: 0 },  // 0 = index of the correct button in "choices"
on_finish: function (data) {
  data.correct = (data.response === data.correct_response);
}
```
:::

A working demo is provided in `button_response_demo.html`.

---

## Summary

Today you extended last week's jsPsych foundations into something that looks like a real task:

- **Multiple trial types** can live in the same timeline, including images.
- **`data`** attaches information to a trial that gets saved but doesn't affect what's shown.
- **A fixation cross before every stimulus** gives participants a consistent point to look at and makes trial changes unambiguous.
- **`jsPsych.randomization.shuffle()`** randomizes stimulus order, reusing what you know about arrays.
- **Functions as parameters** (`stimulus: function() {...}`) let a trial adapt to what just happened, via `on_finish` and `jsPsych.data.get()`.
- **Practice and main blocks**, and repeating a block with a loop, give an experiment real structure.

In Session 3, we'll turn this into something that could actually collect real data: adding a participant-info screen, saving data to a file, computing accuracy and reaction time, and introducing jsPsych's own `timeline_variables` as a cleaner way to do the repetition you built by hand today.

::: {.callout-note}
